title: Titrations and Molar Concentrations
description: Calculate molar concentrations, convert between moles and volumes, and solve full titration problems using mole ratios.

method_card.title: Titrations and Molar Concentrations
method_card.content:
Titration calculations always follow the same four-step pattern. Once you see it, every question is the same shape.

The pattern:

  1. Find the moles of the substance you know (the one where you have both concentration and volume)
  2. Use the balanced equation to find the moles of the substance you don't know (mole ratio)
  3. Use those moles with the other volume to find concentration

Common pitfalls:

  • Volumes in titrations are given in cm³ — you must divide by 1000 to get dm³ before using the concentration formula
  • Always check the mole ratio from the balanced equation — it is not always 1:1
  • If the question gives you a mass, find moles first using moles = mass ÷ Mr
  • If a solution is made up in a volumetric flask (e.g. 250 cm³), the concentration applies to the whole flask, but you only take 25 cm³ for titration
steps: Convert all volumes from cm³ to dm³ (divide by 1000)
Find moles of the known substance: moles = concentration × volume
Use the mole ratio from the balanced equation to find moles of the unknown
Calculate concentration of the unknown: concentration = moles ÷ volume

exam_context.frequency: High — titration calculations appear almost every year in Separate Chemistry

worked_examples.question: A solution has a concentration of 0.5 mol/dm³. Calculate the number of moles in 250 cm³ of this solution.
25.0 cm³ of NaOH is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of HCl with a concentration of 0.125 mol/dm³. The equation is: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the NaOH.

steps.label: Step 2 — Use mole ratio
steps.content:
From the equation: HCl : NaOH = 1 : 1

So moles NaOH = 0.0025 mol

worked_examples.question: 5.3 g of Na₂CO₃ is dissolved in water and made up to 250 cm³ in a volumetric flask. 25.0 cm³ of this solution is titrated against HCl. The titre is 25.0 cm³. The equation is: Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. Calculate the concentration of the HCl in mol/dm³. (Ar: Na = 23, C = 12, O = 16)

steps.label: Step 2 — Find moles of Na₂CO₃ in the flask
Step 4 — Find moles of Na₂CO₃ in the 25.0 cm³ sample
Step 5 — Use mole ratio to find moles of HCl

bronze.display: A solution has a concentration of 0.1 mol/dm³. Calculate the number of moles in 25.0 cm³ of this solution.

misconceptions.message: Convert cm³ to dm³ first: 25.0 ÷ 1000 = 0.025 dm³. Then moles = 0.1 × 0.025 = 0.0025 mol.
Did you divide the volume by 1000? 25 cm³ = 0.025 dm³, not 25 dm³.

bronze.display: 0.5 mol of a solute is dissolved in 0.25 dm³ of solution. Calculate the concentration in mol/dm³.

misconceptions.message: Concentration = moles ÷ volume = 0.5 ÷ 0.25 = 2 mol/dm³. Don't multiply.

bronze.display: A solution has a concentration of 0.5 mol/dm³. What volume (in dm³) is needed to contain 0.2 mol?

misconceptions.message: Rearrange: volume = moles ÷ concentration = 0.2 ÷ 0.5 = 0.4 dm³.

bronze.display: 4.0 g of NaOH is dissolved in 500 cm³ of water. Calculate the number of moles of NaOH. (Ar: Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1)

misconceptions.message: Mr of NaOH = 23 + 16 + 1 = 40. Moles = 4.0 ÷ 40 = 0.1 mol.

bronze.display: A solution contains 0.15 mol of solute in 500 cm³. Calculate the concentration in mol/dm³.

misconceptions.message: Convert volume first: 500 cm³ = 0.5 dm³. Concentration = 0.15 ÷ 0.5 = 0.3 mol/dm³.

bronze.display: Calculate the number of moles in 100 cm³ of a 0.25 mol/dm³ solution.
Convert 50 cm³ to dm³.

misconceptions.message: Divide by 1000, not 100. 50 cm³ ÷ 1000 = 0.05 dm³.

bronze.display: 2.0 g of HCl is dissolved in water. Calculate the number of moles. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (Ar: H = 1, Cl = 35.5)

silver.display: 25.0 cm³ of NaOH of unknown concentration is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.125 mol/dm³ HCl. The equation is: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the NaOH in mol/dm³.
silver.equation_hint: \(n = c \times V\) then use mole ratio, then \(c = \frac{n}{V}\)

misconceptions.message: Convert volumes to dm³: 20.0 cm³ = 0.02 dm³, 25.0 cm³ = 0.025 dm³. Moles HCl = 0.125 × 0.02 = 0.0025. Ratio 1:1, so moles NaOH = 0.0025. Conc = 0.0025 ÷ 0.025 = 0.1 mol/dm³.
Use the NaOH volume (25.0 cm³) for the final step, not the HCl volume.

silver.display: 25.0 cm³ of 0.2 mol/dm³ NaOH is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of H₂SO₄. The equation is: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the H₂SO₄ in mol/dm³.
silver.equation_hint: \(n = c \times V\) then use mole ratio

misconceptions.message: The ratio is 1:2 (H₂SO₄ : NaOH). Moles NaOH = 0.2 × 0.025 = 0.005. Moles H₂SO₄ = 0.005 ÷ 2 = 0.0025. Conc = 0.0025 ÷ 0.02 = 0.125 mol/dm³.
Don't forget the 2:1 ratio. You need half as many moles of H₂SO₄ as NaOH.

silver.display: 25.0 cm³ of 0.15 mol/dm³ HCl is neutralised by 18.75 cm³ of NaOH. The equation is: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the NaOH in mol/dm³.

misconceptions.message: Use the NaOH volume for the final step. Moles HCl = 0.15 × 0.025 = 0.00375. Ratio 1:1. Conc NaOH = 0.00375 ÷ 0.01875 = 0.2 mol/dm³.

silver.display: 25.0 cm³ of 0.1 mol/dm³ Ca(OH)₂ is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of HCl. The equation is: Ca(OH)₂ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + 2H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the HCl in mol/dm³.
silver.equation_hint: \(n = c \times V\) then use mole ratio

misconceptions.message: The equation shows 2 moles of HCl per mole of Ca(OH)₂, so double the moles.

silver.display: 25.0 cm³ of 0.2 mol/dm³ KOH is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of HNO₃. The equation is: KOH + HNO₃ → KNO₃ + H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the HNO₃ in mol/dm³.

misconceptions.message: Moles KOH = 0.2 × 0.025 = 0.005. Ratio 1:1. Conc HNO₃ = 0.005 ÷ 0.02 = 0.25 mol/dm³.

silver.display: 25.0 cm³ of 0.5 mol/dm³ KOH is neutralised by 25.0 cm³ of H₂SO₄. The equation is: H₂SO₄ + 2KOH → K₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the H₂SO₄ in mol/dm³.
silver.equation_hint: \(n = c \times V\) then use mole ratio

misconceptions.message: Two moles of KOH react with one mole of H₂SO₄. Halve the moles of KOH.

gold.display: 2.0 g of NaOH (Mr = 40) is dissolved in water and made up to 200 cm³ in a volumetric flask. 25.0 cm³ of this solution is titrated against HCl. The titre is 31.25 cm³. The equation is: NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the HCl in mol/dm³.

misconceptions.message: First find moles NaOH = 2/40 = 0.05 mol. Conc in flask = 0.05/0.2 = 0.25 mol/dm³. Moles in 25cm³ = 0.25 × 0.025 = 0.00625. Conc HCl = 0.00625/0.03125 = 0.2 mol/dm³.
The 200 cm³ is the total flask volume. You only use 25.0 cm³ in the titration.

gold.display: 5.3 g of Na₂CO₃ is dissolved in water and made up to 250 cm³. 25.0 cm³ of this solution is titrated against HCl, and the titre is 25.0 cm³. The equation is: Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. Calculate the concentration of the HCl in mol/dm³. (Ar: Na = 23, C = 12, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: Na₂CO₃ : HCl = 1 : 2. You need double the moles of HCl.

gold.display: Calculate the mass of hydrogen chloride (HCl) needed to make 250 cm³ of a 0.5 mol/dm³ solution. Give your answer to 1 decimal place. (Ar: H = 1, Cl = 35.5)

A student dissolves some KOH in water and makes up 500 cm³ of solution. A 25.0 cm³ sample is titrated with 20.0 cm³ of 0.1 mol/dm³ HCl. KOH + HCl → KCl + H₂O. Calculate the mass of KOH originally dissolved. (Ar: K = 39, O = 16, H = 1)

misconceptions.message: Moles HCl = 0.1 × 0.02 = 0.002. 1:1 ratio, so moles KOH in 25cm³ = 0.002. Conc KOH = 0.002/0.025 = 0.08 mol/dm³. Total moles in 500cm³ = 0.08 × 0.5 = 0.04 mol. Mr KOH = 56. Mass = 0.04 × 56 = 2.24 g.
The titration uses 25 cm³ from a 500 cm³ flask. Scale up: total moles = conc × 0.5 dm³.

gold.display: A student dissolves some NaOH in water and makes 250 cm³ of solution. 25.0 cm³ of this is titrated with 20.0 cm³ of 0.2 mol/dm³ HNO₃. NaOH + HNO₃ → NaNO₃ + H₂O. Calculate the mass of NaOH dissolved. (Ar: Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1)

misconceptions.message: Moles HNO₃ = 0.2 × 0.02 = 0.004. 1:1 ratio. Conc NaOH = 0.004/0.025 = 0.16 mol/dm³. Total moles = 0.16 × 0.25 = 0.04. Mr NaOH = 40. Mass = 0.04 × 40 = 1.6 g.
You titrated 25 cm³ from a 250 cm³ flask. Multiply the sample moles by 10 to get the total.

gold.display: A student dissolves Na₂CO₃ in water and makes up 500 cm³ of solution. 25.0 cm³ of this is titrated with 12.5 cm³ of 0.1 mol/dm³ H₂SO₄. The equation is: Na₂CO₃ + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + H₂O + CO₂. Calculate the mass of Na₂CO₃ originally dissolved. (Ar: Na = 23, C = 12, O = 16)

title: Gas Volumes and Atom Economy
description: Calculate gas volumes at RTP using molar volume, compare atom economies of different reaction routes, and calculate percentage yield.

method_card.title: Gas Volumes and Atom Economy
method_card.content:
Three different calculations that test different ideas.

Gas volumes at RTP: At room temperature and pressure, one mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³ (24,000 cm³). This is a universal constant — it doesn't matter which gas. If the question involves a gas, you'll almost certainly need this.

Atom economy: This is about the equation, not the experiment. It tells you what fraction of the atoms end up in the desired product. A high atom economy means less waste by design. Always use the balanced equation — never actual experimental masses.

Percentage yield: This is about the experiment. It compares what you actually got to what you could theoretically have got. Yield is always less than 100% because of incomplete reactions, side reactions, or transfer losses.

Common pitfalls:

  • Atom economy uses Mr of all products in the denominator — not reactants
  • Molar volume is 24 dm³ — if you want cm³, multiply by 1000
  • For gas volume from equations, find moles of gas using stoichiometry first
steps: Identify which calculation: gas volume, atom economy, or percentage yield
For gas volume: find moles of gas (from equation), then multiply by 24
For atom economy: find Mr of desired product ÷ Mr of ALL products × 100
For yield: actual mass ÷ theoretical mass × 100

exam_context.frequency: High — atom economy and gas volumes are common in Separate Chemistry

worked_examples.question: Calculate the volume of 0.5 mol of carbon dioxide gas at RTP.

steps.label: Step 1 — Recall molar volume
steps.content: At RTP, 1 mol of any gas occupies 24 dm³

worked_examples.question: 5.0 g of calcium carbonate decomposes: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. Calculate the volume of CO₂ produced at RTP. (Ar: Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)
3.25 g of zinc reacts with excess hydrochloric acid: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. The student collects 960 cm³ of hydrogen gas at RTP. Calculate the percentage yield. (Ar: Zn = 65)

steps.label: Step 2 — Find theoretical moles of H₂

bronze.display: Calculate the volume occupied by 0.5 mol of hydrogen gas at RTP. Give your answer in dm³.

misconceptions.message: At RTP, 1 mole of any gas = 24 dm³. Volume = 0.5 × 24 = 12 dm³.

bronze.display: A gas has a volume of 4.8 dm³ at RTP. Calculate the number of moles of gas.

misconceptions.message: Moles = volume ÷ 24 = 4.8 ÷ 24 = 0.2 mol. Don't multiply.

bronze.display: Calculate the volume of 2 mol of oxygen gas at RTP in dm³.

misconceptions.message: Volume = moles × 24 = 2 × 24 = 48 dm³.

bronze.display: In the reaction CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂, the only desired product is CaO. Calculate the atom economy. (Mr: CaO = 56, CO₂ = 44)
bronze.equation_hint: \(\text{atom economy} = \frac{M_r \text{ of desired product}}{M_r \text{ of all products}} \times 100\)

misconceptions.message: Use Mr of ALL products: 56 + 44 = 100. Atom economy = (56/100) × 100 = 56%. Don't use reactant Mr.

bronze.display: In the reaction 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, the desired product is MgO. Calculate the atom economy.
bronze.equation_hint: \(\text{atom economy} = \frac{M_r \text{ of desired product}}{M_r \text{ of all products}} \times 100\)

misconceptions.message: There is only one product (MgO), so all atoms end up in the desired product. Atom economy = 100%.

bronze.display: A student expected to make 10 g of a salt but only obtained 7.5 g. Calculate the percentage yield.

misconceptions.message: Percentage yield = (actual ÷ theoretical) × 100 = (7.5 ÷ 10) × 100 = 75%.

bronze.display: In the reaction 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂, 0.1 mol of H₂O₂ decomposes. Calculate the volume of O₂ produced at RTP in dm³.

misconceptions.message: From the equation, 2 mol H₂O₂ → 1 mol O₂. So 0.1 mol H₂O₂ → 0.05 mol O₂. Volume = 0.05 × 24 = 1.2 dm³.

bronze.display: A gas occupies 7.2 dm³ at RTP. Calculate the number of moles of gas.

misconceptions.message: Moles = volume ÷ 24 = 7.2 ÷ 24 = 0.3 mol.
Divide by 24, don't multiply. Moles = 7.2 ÷ 24 = 0.3 mol.

silver.display: 5.0 g of calcium carbonate decomposes: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. Calculate the volume of CO₂ produced at RTP in dm³. (Mr: CaCO₃ = 100)

misconceptions.message: Moles CaCO₃ = 5/100 = 0.05. Ratio 1:1, so moles CO₂ = 0.05. Volume = 0.05 × 24 = 1.2 dm³.

silver.display: 2.3 g of sodium reacts with water: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. Calculate the volume of hydrogen gas produced at RTP in dm³. (Ar: Na = 23)

misconceptions.message: Moles Na = 2.3/23 = 0.1. From equation: 2Na → 1H₂, so moles H₂ = 0.1/2 = 0.05. Volume = 0.05 × 24 = 1.2 dm³.
2 moles of Na produce 1 mole of H₂. Halve the moles of Na.

silver.display: 0.6 g of magnesium reacts with excess HCl: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. Calculate the volume of hydrogen produced at RTP in dm³. (Ar: Mg = 24)

misconceptions.message: Moles Mg = 0.6/24 = 0.025. Ratio 1:1 for Mg:H₂. Volume = 0.025 × 24 = 0.6 dm³.

silver.display: 10 g of iron(III) oxide is reduced: 2Fe₂O₃ + 3C → 4Fe + 3CO₂. The student obtains 5.6 g of iron. Calculate the percentage yield. (Mr: Fe₂O₃ = 160, Ar: Fe = 56)

misconceptions.message: Moles Fe₂O₃ = 10/160 = 0.0625. From equation: 2 mol Fe₂O₃ → 4 mol Fe, so 0.0625 → 0.125 mol Fe. Theoretical mass = 0.125 × 56 = 7.0 g. Yield = (5.6/7.0) × 100 = 80%.
The ratio is 2 Fe₂O₃ : 4 Fe, which simplifies to 1 : 2. Double the moles.

silver.display: In the reaction Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂, the desired product is iron. Calculate the atom economy. (Mr: Fe = 56, CO₂ = 44)
silver.equation_hint: \(\text{atom economy} = \frac{M_r \text{ of desired}}{M_r \text{ of all products}} \times 100\)

misconceptions.message: Don't forget the coefficients. It's 2 moles of Fe (Mr = 112) and 3 moles of CO₂ (Mr = 132).

silver.display: In the reaction N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, the desired product is ammonia. Calculate the atom economy.
silver.equation_hint: \(\text{atom economy} = \frac{M_r \text{ of desired}}{M_r \text{ of all products}} \times 100\)

misconceptions.message: NH₃ is the only product. When there is only one product, atom economy = 100%.

gold.display: 3.25 g of zinc reacts with excess HCl: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. The student collects 960 cm³ of hydrogen at RTP. Calculate the percentage yield. (Ar: Zn = 65)

misconceptions.message: Moles Zn = 3.25/65 = 0.05. Ratio 1:1, so moles H₂ = 0.05. Theoretical volume = 0.05 × 24 = 1.2 dm³ = 1200 cm³. Yield = (960/1200) × 100 = 80%.
Convert to the same units. 960 cm³ and 1200 cm³, or 0.96 dm³ and 1.2 dm³.

gold.display: Two routes can produce calcium oxide (CaO). Route A: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ (Mr: CaO = 56, CO₂ = 44). Route B: Ca(OH)₂ → CaO + H₂O (Mr: CaO = 56, H₂O = 18). Calculate the atom economy for Route B. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

misconceptions.message: Route B: Mr of all products = 56 + 18 = 74. AE = (56/74) × 100 = 75.7%. Route A would be 56%.
Use Mr of all products (56 + 18 = 74), not Mr of reactant.

gold.display: 32 g of iron(III) oxide reacts with carbon monoxide: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Calculate the volume of CO₂ produced at RTP. (Mr: Fe₂O₃ = 160)

misconceptions.message: Moles Fe₂O₃ = 32/160 = 0.2. From equation: 1 Fe₂O₃ → 3 CO₂. Moles CO₂ = 0.2 × 3 = 0.6. Volume = 0.6 × 24 = 14.4 dm³.
1 mole of Fe₂O₃ produces 3 moles of CO₂. Multiply by 3.

gold.display: 12.25 g of potassium chlorate decomposes: 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂. Calculate the volume of oxygen produced at RTP. (Ar: K = 39, Cl = 35.5, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: Mr KClO₃ = 39 + 35.5 + (3×16) = 122.5. Moles = 12.25/122.5 = 0.1. From equation: 2KClO₃ → 3O₂, so 0.1 mol → 0.15 mol O₂. Volume = 0.15 × 24 = 3.6 dm³.
The ratio is 2 : 3 (KClO₃ : O₂). 0.1 mol KClO₃ gives 0.1 × 3/2 = 0.15 mol O₂.

gold.display: 2.5 g of CaCO₃ reacts with excess HCl: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂. The student collects 504 cm³ of CO₂ at RTP. Calculate the percentage yield. (Mr: CaCO₃ = 100)

misconceptions.message: Moles CaCO₃ = 2.5/100 = 0.025. 1:1 ratio, moles CO₂ = 0.025. Theoretical volume = 0.025 × 24 = 0.6 dm³ = 600 cm³. Yield = (504/600) × 100 = 84%.
Convert: 504 cm³ and 600 cm³ (or 0.504 dm³ and 0.6 dm³).

gold.display: In the decomposition 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂, the desired product is oxygen. Calculate the atom economy. (Ar: K = 39, Cl = 35.5, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: Don't use Mr of reactants. Use Mr of ALL products: 2KCl + 3O₂ = 149 + 96 = 245.

title: Moments, Levers and Gears
description: Calculate moments, solve balanced beam problems using the principle of moments, and analyse gear ratios for force and speed.

method_card.title: Moments, Levers and Gears
method_card.content:
A moment is the turning effect of a force. Every moment question follows the same approach — but you must be careful about which distance you use.

Key strategies:

  • Distance must always be measured perpendicular to the line of action of the force, from the pivot
  • For a balanced beam, the total clockwise moment equals the total anticlockwise moment — set them equal and solve
  • If a question mentions weight, you may need to calculate it first using W = mg
  • For multiple forces on one side, calculate each moment separately and add them

Gears:

  • A larger gear turns slower but with more force (torque)
  • Gear ratio = driven teeth ÷ driver teeth
  • The driven gear always turns in the opposite direction
steps: Identify the pivot point and which forces are clockwise vs anticlockwise
Calculate W = mg if you're given mass instead of force
For balanced beams: set clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment
For gears: gear ratio = teeth on driven ÷ teeth on driver

worked_examples.question: A force of 50 N acts at a perpendicular distance of 0.3 m from a pivot. Calculate the moment.
A child of mass 30 kg sits 2.0 m from the pivot of a seesaw. An adult of mass 60 kg sits on the other side. How far from the pivot must the adult sit to balance the seesaw? (g = 9.8 N/kg)

A uniform beam is 2.0 m long and has a mass of 10 kg. The pivot is 0.8 m from the left end. A 50 N load hangs from the left end. Calculate the force needed at the right end to balance the beam. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

steps.label: Step 1 — Find weight of beam
steps.content: W = 10 × 9.8 = 98 N, acting at the centre (1.0 m from left end)

steps.label: Step 2 — Find distances from pivot
steps.content:
50 N load: 0.8 m from pivot (anticlockwise)

Beam weight 98 N: centre is at 1.0 m from left, so 1.0 − 0.8 = 0.2 m from pivot (clockwise)

Unknown force F: 2.0 − 0.8 = 1.2 m from pivot (clockwise)

bronze.display: A force of 50 N acts at a perpendicular distance of 0.3 m from a pivot. Calculate the moment.

misconceptions.message: Moment = force × distance = 50 × 0.3 = 15 Nm.

bronze.display: A moment of 20 Nm is produced by a force acting 0.4 m from a pivot. Calculate the force.

misconceptions.message: Rearrange: F = M ÷ d = 20 ÷ 0.4 = 50 N.

bronze.display: A force of 30 N creates a moment of 12 Nm. Calculate the perpendicular distance from the pivot.
A spanner applies a force of 200 N at a distance of 1.5 m from the bolt. Calculate the moment about the bolt.
A moment of 36 Nm acts on a door handle. The handle is 0.6 m from the hinge. Calculate the force applied.
A force of 80 N acts at a perpendicular distance of 0.25 m from a pivot. Calculate the moment.

misconceptions.message: Moment = 80 × 0.25 = 20 Nm.

bronze.display: A force of 15 N creates a moment of 45 Nm. Calculate the perpendicular distance from the pivot.
A seesaw is balanced. A 400 N force acts 2.0 m from the pivot on the left. A force acts 1.6 m from the pivot on the right. What is the force on the right?

silver.display: A child of mass 30 kg sits 2.0 m from the pivot of a seesaw. An adult of mass 60 kg sits on the other side. How far from the pivot must the adult sit to balance? (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: First find weights: child = 30 × 9.8 = 294 N, adult = 60 × 9.8 = 588 N. Then 294 × 2 = 588 × d. d = 588/588 = 1.0 m.
Use weight (W = mg), not mass, in the moment equation.

silver.display: A 600 N force acts 0.8 m from a pivot (clockwise). What force at 1.2 m from the pivot (anticlockwise) is needed to balance it?

A nutcracker has the nut 0.08 m from the pivot and the handle 0.4 m from the pivot. A 5 kg mass is placed in the nutcracker. Calculate the force you need to apply at the handle to crack it. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Convert mass to weight first: W = mg = 5 × 9.8 = 49 N.

silver.display: A beam has a pivot in the centre. A 200 N force acts 1.0 m to the left of the pivot. A 150 N force acts 2.0 m to the right. Calculate the resultant moment. State the direction (clockwise or anticlockwise). Give your answer as the magnitude only.

misconceptions.message: ACW moment = 200 × 1 = 200 Nm. CW moment = 150 × 2 = 300 Nm. Resultant = 300 − 200 = 100 Nm clockwise.

silver.display: An 8 kg mass hangs from a horizontal bar at a distance of 0.25 m from the pivot. Calculate the moment about the pivot. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: First find weight: W = 8 × 9.8 = 78.4 N. Moment = 78.4 × 0.25 = 19.6 Nm.

silver.display: A wheelbarrow has its load of 150 N at 0.4 m from the wheel (pivot). The handles are 1.2 m from the wheel. Calculate the effort needed at the handles to lift the load.

misconceptions.message: Load × load distance = effort × effort distance. 150 × 0.4 = F × 1.2. F = 60 ÷ 1.2 = 50 N.

gold.display: A beam is balanced on a pivot. On the left side: a 100 N force acts 0.5 m from the pivot, and a 200 N force acts 1.5 m from the pivot. What single force on the right, at 0.7 m from the pivot, is needed to balance the beam?

misconceptions.message: With multiple forces on one side, calculate each moment separately then add: (100 × 0.5) + (200 × 1.5) = 350 Nm.

gold.display: A gear system has a driver gear with 20 teeth and a driven gear with 60 teeth. The driver gear rotates at 120 rpm. Calculate the speed of the driven gear in rpm.

misconceptions.message: Gear ratio = 60/20 = 3. The driven gear turns 3× slower: 120 ÷ 3 = 40 rpm.
A larger driven gear turns SLOWER. Divide the speed by the gear ratio, don't multiply.

gold.display: A gear system has a driver gear with 20 teeth and a driven gear with 60 teeth. If the input force is 15 N, calculate the output force (assuming no energy losses).

misconceptions.message: Gear ratio = 60/20 = 3. The driven gear has 3× more force: 15 × 3 = 45 N. Larger gear = more force.
A larger driven gear multiplies force. Multiply by the gear ratio, not divide.

gold.display: A uniform beam is 2.0 m long with mass 10 kg. The pivot is 0.8 m from the left end. A 50 N load hangs from the left end. Calculate the force needed at the right end to balance the beam. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Beam weight = 10 × 9.8 = 98 N at centre (1.0 m from left = 0.2 m right of pivot). ACW = 50 × 0.8 = 40 Nm. CW = 98 × 0.2 = 19.6 Nm + F × 1.2. So 40 = 19.6 + 1.2F. F = 20.4/1.2 = 17 N.
A uniform beam's weight acts at its centre. The centre is 1.0 m from the left end.

gold.display: A lever is connected to an input gear with 15 teeth. A force of 12 N is applied 0.3 m from the pivot on the lever. The output gear has 45 teeth. Calculate the output torque (moment) from the gear system in Nm.

misconceptions.message: Input torque = 12 × 0.3 = 3.6 Nm. Gear ratio = 45/15 = 3. Output torque = 3.6 × 3 = 10.8 Nm.
More teeth on output = more torque. Multiply the input torque by the gear ratio.

gold.display: A crowbar is used to lift a heavy stone. The effort of 80 N is applied 0.75 m from the pivot. The stone rests 0.05 m from the pivot. Calculate the maximum force exerted on the stone.

misconceptions.message: Effort × effort distance = load × load distance. 80 × 0.75 = F × 0.05. F = 60 ÷ 0.05 = 1200 N.
The load is closer to the pivot, so the force is multiplied. Mechanical advantage = 0.75/0.05 = 15.

title: Pressure in Fluids
description: Calculate pressure using p = F/A for solid surfaces and p = hρg for fluids, including unit conversions and total pressure at depth.

method_card.title: Pressure in Fluids
method_card.content:
There are two different pressure equations and you must pick the right one for the situation.

Solid on a surface: Use the recall equation. Force is the weight of the object, area is the contact area. This is a recall equation — you must memorise it.

Liquid pressure: Pressure increases with depth. This equation is on the physics equation sheet. Depth must be in metres, density in kg/m³.

Common pitfalls:

  • Convert cm² to m² by dividing by 10,000 (not 100)
  • Convert cm to m by dividing by 100
  • For total pressure at depth in a liquid, you must add atmospheric pressure (≈ 101,000 Pa) to the liquid pressure
  • Remember: 1 kPa = 1000 Pa
steps: Identify which equation: p = F/A (solid surface) or p = hρg (liquid)
Convert all units: cm² → m² (÷10,000), cm → m (÷100), g → kg (÷1000)
Substitute values and calculate
For total pressure at depth: add atmospheric pressure (101,000 Pa)

exam_context.frequency: Common — pressure appears on most Paper 1 exams

worked_examples.question: A box weighing 200 N rests on the floor. The area of the base is 0.04 m². Calculate the pressure on the floor.
A column of mercury is 0.8 m tall. The density of mercury is 13,600 kg/m³. Calculate the pressure at the bottom of the column. (g = 9.8 N/kg)
A diver is 25 m below the surface of the sea. The density of seawater is 1025 kg/m³. Calculate the total pressure on the diver. (g = 9.8 N/kg, atmospheric pressure = 101,000 Pa)

bronze.display: A box weighing 200 N rests on the floor. The area of the base is 0.04 m². Calculate the pressure on the floor.

misconceptions.message: Pressure = force ÷ area = 200 ÷ 0.04 = 5000 Pa. Don't multiply.

bronze.display: Calculate the pressure at the bottom of a 2 m deep swimming pool. The density of water is 1000 kg/m³. (g = 9.8 N/kg)
bronze.equation_hint: Given on equation sheet: \(p = h\rho g\)

misconceptions.message: Use p = hρg for liquids: p = 2 × 1000 × 9.8 = 19,600 Pa.

bronze.display: A pressure of 50,000 Pa acts over an area of 0.1 m². Calculate the force.
A crate weighing 500 N rests on the ground with a base area of 0.05 m². Calculate the pressure.
Calculate the pressure at a depth of 5 m in water. Density of water = 1000 kg/m³. (g = 9.8 N/kg)
bronze.equation_hint: Given on equation sheet: \(p = h\rho g\)

bronze.display: A 600 N force creates a pressure of 3000 Pa. Calculate the area over which it acts.
The pressure at the bottom of a column of liquid is 29,400 Pa. The density is 1000 kg/m³. Calculate the depth. (g = 9.8 N/kg)
A pressure of 800 Pa acts on an area of 0.5 m². Calculate the force.

silver.display: A person weighing 300 N stands on a surface 20 cm × 50 cm. Calculate the pressure in Pa. (Give your answer as a whole number.)

misconceptions.message: Convert to metres: 0.20 m × 0.50 m = 0.1 m². Pressure = 300 ÷ 0.1 = 3000 Pa.
Area must be in m². 20 cm = 0.2 m, 50 cm = 0.5 m. Area = 0.2 × 0.5 = 0.1 m².

silver.display: A column of mercury (density 13,600 kg/m³) is 0.8 m tall. Calculate the pressure at the bottom in Pa. (g = 9.8 N/kg)
silver.equation_hint: Given on equation sheet: \(p = h\rho g\)

misconceptions.message: Use the density of mercury (13,600 kg/m³), not water. p = 0.8 × 13,600 × 9.8 = 106,624 Pa.

silver.display: Calculate the total pressure on a diver at 10 m depth in water (density 1000 kg/m³). Include atmospheric pressure of 101,000 Pa. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Liquid pressure = 10 × 1000 × 9.8 = 98,000 Pa. Total = 101,000 + 98,000 = 199,000 Pa. Don't forget atmospheric pressure.

silver.display: A nail pushes with a force of 50 N. The point of the nail has an area of 2 cm². Calculate the pressure in Pa.

misconceptions.message: Convert cm² to m²: 2 cm² = 2 ÷ 10,000 = 0.0002 m². Pressure = 50 ÷ 0.0002 = 250,000 Pa.
To convert cm² to m², divide by 10,000 (not 100). 1 m² = 10,000 cm².

silver.display: The pressure at the bottom of a tank of liquid is 34,300 Pa. The depth is 3.5 m. Calculate the density of the liquid. (g = 9.8 N/kg)
Calculate the difference in pressure between a depth of 3 m and 8 m in water (density 1000 kg/m³). (g = 9.8 N/kg)
silver.equation_hint: Given on equation sheet: \(p = h\rho g\)

misconceptions.message: Use the depth difference: Δh = 8 − 3 = 5 m. Δp = 5 × 1000 × 9.8 = 49,000 Pa.

gold.display: A diver is 25 m below the surface of the sea (density 1025 kg/m³). Calculate the total pressure on the diver. Atmospheric pressure = 101,000 Pa. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Use the density of seawater (1025 kg/m³), not fresh water (1000 kg/m³).

gold.display: A cuboid of mass 20 kg has dimensions 0.5 m × 0.2 m × 0.1 m. Calculate the maximum pressure it can exert on the floor. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Weight = 20 × 9.8 = 196 N. Maximum pressure = smallest area face. Smallest area = 0.2 × 0.1 = 0.02 m². p = 196/0.02 = 9800 Pa.
For MAXIMUM pressure, use the SMALLEST face (0.2 × 0.1 = 0.02 m²), not the largest.

gold.display: A dam holds back water 40 m deep. Calculate the force on a gate at the bottom of the dam that is 2 m wide and 1.5 m tall. Use the pressure at the full 40 m depth. (density of water = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Area of the gate = 2 × 1.5 = 3 m². Force = pressure × area.

gold.display: In a hydraulic system, the small piston has an area of 0.002 m² and the large piston has an area of 0.04 m². A force of 50 N is applied to the small piston. Calculate the force exerted by the large piston.

misconceptions.message: Pressure in fluid = F/A = 50/0.002 = 25,000 Pa. Same pressure on large piston: F = 25,000 × 0.04 = 1000 N.
The large piston has a LARGER area, so the force is MULTIPLIED. F₂ = F₁ × (A₂/A₁) = 50 × (0.04/0.002) = 1000 N.

gold.display: A tank contains oil with a density of 800 kg/m³. At what depth does the pressure due to the oil equal atmospheric pressure (101,000 Pa)? Give your answer to 1 decimal place. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Use the density of oil (800 kg/m³), not water.

gold.display: A submarine is 200 m below the surface of the sea (density of seawater = 1025 kg/m³). Calculate the total pressure on the hull in kPa. Atmospheric pressure = 101,000 Pa. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Convert Pa to kPa: divide by 1000. 2,110,000 Pa = 2110 kPa.

title: Nuclear Equations and Half-Life
description: Balance nuclear equations for alpha and beta decay, and calculate remaining activity or mass after multiple half-lives.

method_card.title: Nuclear Equations and Half-Life
method_card.content:
Two different skills that look very different but both come down to counting.

Nuclear equations: Both the top numbers (mass numbers) and the bottom numbers (atomic numbers) must balance on each side. This lets you fill in any missing value.

  • Alpha decay: emits a helium nucleus — mass number drops by 4, atomic number drops by 2
  • Beta decay: a neutron turns into a proton — mass number stays the same, atomic number goes up by 1

Half-life: The time for half the radioactive nuclei to decay. There is no equation to learn — just keep halving.

  • Count how many times you halve to reach the target value
  • Each halving = one half-life
  • To find the half-life: total time ÷ number of halvings
  • After \(n\) half-lives, the fraction remaining = \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n\)
steps: For nuclear equations: check both mass number and atomic number balance
Alpha: mass −4, atomic number −2. Beta: mass same, atomic number +1
For half-life: keep halving the initial value until you reach the target
Count the halvings, then use: half-life = total time ÷ number of halvings

exam_context.frequency: High — nuclear equations and half-life appear on almost every Paper 1

worked_examples.question: Radium-226 (atomic number 88) undergoes alpha decay. What is the mass number of the daughter nucleus?

steps.label: Step 1 — Recall alpha decay
steps.content: Alpha decay: mass number drops by 4, atomic number drops by 2

worked_examples.question: A radioactive source has an activity of 6400 Bq. After 20 minutes, the activity is 400 Bq. Calculate the half-life.
A radioactive sample has an activity of 5000 Bq. After 52 days, the activity is 312.5 Bq. Calculate the half-life in days.

bronze.display: Radium-226 (atomic number 88) undergoes alpha decay. What is the mass number of the daughter nucleus?

misconceptions.message: Alpha decay reduces mass number by 4: 226 − 4 = 222.
Alpha decay changes the mass number. Beta decay does not. Mass = 226 − 4 = 222.

bronze.display: Radium-226 (atomic number 88) undergoes alpha decay. What is the atomic number of the daughter nucleus?

misconceptions.message: Alpha decay reduces atomic number by 2: 88 − 2 = 86 (radon).

bronze.display: Carbon-14 (atomic number 6) undergoes beta decay. What is the atomic number of the daughter nucleus?
bronze.equation_hint: Beta: mass stays same, atomic number +1

misconceptions.message: Beta decay increases atomic number by 1: 6 + 1 = 7 (nitrogen).
In beta decay, a neutron becomes a proton. Atomic number goes UP by 1.

bronze.display: A radioactive source has an activity of 800 Bq. What is the activity after 4 half-lives?
bronze.equation_hint: Halve the activity for each half-life

misconceptions.message: 800 → 400 → 200 → 100 → 50 Bq. Each arrow is one half-life. After 4 half-lives: 50 Bq.

bronze.display: A radioactive source has an initial activity of 2000 Bq. Calculate the activity after 3 half-lives.
bronze.equation_hint: Halve the activity for each half-life

misconceptions.message: 2000 → 1000 → 500 → 250 Bq. After 3 half-lives: 250 Bq.

bronze.display: Uranium-238 (atomic number 92) undergoes alpha decay. What is the mass number of the daughter nucleus?

misconceptions.message: Alpha: mass drops by 4. 238 − 4 = 234 (thorium-234).

bronze.display: Lead-214 (atomic number 82) undergoes beta decay. What is the atomic number of the daughter nucleus?
bronze.equation_hint: Beta: mass stays same, atomic number +1

misconceptions.message: Beta: atomic number increases by 1. 82 + 1 = 83 (bismuth-214).

bronze.display: Cobalt-60 (atomic number 27) undergoes beta decay. What is the atomic number of the daughter nucleus?
bronze.equation_hint: Beta: mass stays same, atomic number +1

misconceptions.message: Beta: atomic number increases by 1. 27 + 1 = 28 (nickel-60).
Beta decay does NOT change the mass number. Only the atomic number changes (+1).

silver.display: A radioactive source has an activity of 6400 Bq. After 20 minutes the activity is 400 Bq. Calculate the half-life in minutes.

misconceptions.message: 6400 → 3200 → 1600 → 800 → 400 = 4 halvings. Half-life = 20 ÷ 4 = 5 minutes.
Don't divide the time by the activity. Count how many times you halve to get from 6400 to 400.

silver.display: A radioactive sample initially has an activity of 1200 Bq. After 30 minutes the activity is 150 Bq. Calculate the half-life in minutes.
silver.equation_hint: Count halvings then divide time by number of halvings

misconceptions.message: 1200 → 600 → 300 → 150 = 3 halvings. Half-life = 30 ÷ 3 = 10 minutes.

silver.display: Americium-241 (atomic number 95) undergoes alpha decay. What is the mass number and atomic number of the daughter nucleus? Enter the mass number only.

misconceptions.message: Alpha: mass = 241 − 4 = 237. Atomic = 95 − 2 = 93 (neptunium-237).

silver.display: Strontium-90 (atomic number 38) undergoes beta decay. What is the atomic number of the daughter nucleus?

misconceptions.message: Beta: atomic number + 1. 38 + 1 = 39 (yttrium-90). Mass stays at 90.

silver.display: A 50 g sample of a radioactive isotope has a half-life of 3 hours. What mass remains after 15 hours?
silver.equation_hint: Number of half-lives = total time ÷ half-life

misconceptions.message: You halve each time, not subtract a fixed amount.

silver.display: Polonium-210 (atomic number 84) undergoes alpha decay to form lead. What is the mass number of the lead isotope produced?

misconceptions.message: Alpha: mass = 210 − 4 = 206. Atomic = 84 − 2 = 82 (lead-206).

gold.display: A radioactive sample has an activity of 5000 Bq. After 52 days, the activity is 312.5 Bq. Calculate the half-life in days.

misconceptions.message: 5000 ÷ 312.5 = 16 = 2⁴. So 4 half-lives. Half-life = 52/4 = 13 days.

gold.display: A radioactive isotope has a half-life of 8 hours. What fraction of the original sample remains after 56 hours? Enter as a fraction with denominator only (e.g. for ¼ enter 4).

misconceptions.message: 56 ÷ 8 = 7 half-lives. Fraction remaining = (½)⁷ = 1/128.
Each half-life halves the amount. After 7 half-lives: 2⁷ = 128. Fraction = 1/128.

gold.display: Thorium-234 (atomic number 90) decays to protactinium-234 (atomic number 91). What type of decay is this — alpha or beta? Enter 'alpha' or 'beta'.

misconceptions.message: Mass stays at 234 (no change). Atomic number goes from 90 to 91 (+1). This is beta decay — a neutron has changed into a proton.

gold.display: Sodium-24 (atomic number 11) undergoes beta decay. The daughter nucleus then undergoes alpha decay. What is the final mass number?

misconceptions.message: Beta: mass stays 24, atomic 11 → 12 (magnesium-24). Then alpha: mass 24 − 4 = 20, atomic 12 − 2 = 10 (neon-20). Final mass = 20.
Apply beta first (mass stays, atomic +1), then alpha (mass −4, atomic −2).

gold.display: A radioactive source has an initial count rate of 480 counts per minute (after background subtraction). After 2 hours, the count rate is 30 counts per minute. Calculate the half-life in minutes.

misconceptions.message: 480 → 240 → 120 → 60 → 30 = 4 halvings. 2 hours = 120 minutes. Half-life = 120 ÷ 4 = 30 minutes.
Convert 2 hours to 120 minutes before dividing by the number of halvings.

gold.display: Iodine-131 (atomic number 53) undergoes beta decay. What is the atomic number of the daughter nucleus?

misconceptions.message: Beta decay: atomic number + 1 = 53 + 1 = 54 (xenon-131). Mass stays at 131.

title: Transformers and Electromagnetic Induction
description: Calculate transformer voltages and currents using the turns ratio and power equation, and explain why high voltages reduce National Grid losses.

method_card.title: Transformers and Electromagnetic Induction
method_card.content:
Transformer questions combine two equations — the turns ratio (recall) and the power equation (given on the sheet for 100% efficient transformers).

Strategy:

  1. Use the turns ratio to find the missing voltage
  2. If the question asks about current, use the power equation next

Key ideas:

  • A step-up transformer has more secondary turns than primary — voltage goes up, current goes down
  • A step-down transformer has fewer secondary turns — voltage goes down, current goes up
  • For a 100% efficient transformer, power in = power out. More voltage means less current for the same power

National Grid:

  • Power is transmitted at very high voltage (400 kV) to reduce current
  • Lower current means less energy wasted as heat in cables
  • The key equation for loss is power loss = current² × resistance — current is squared, so halving the current reduces losses by a factor of 4
steps: Use the turns ratio to link voltages: Vp/Vs = np/ns
For current questions: use VpIp = VsIs (100% efficient)
Step-up = more secondary turns = higher voltage = lower current
National Grid: high V → low I → less P = I²R loss

exam_context.frequency: High — transformers appear on almost every Paper 2

worked_examples.question: A transformer has 1000 primary turns and 50 secondary turns. The primary voltage is 230 V. Calculate the secondary voltage.

steps.label: Step 1 — Write the turns ratio equation

worked_examples.question: A transformer has a primary voltage of 230 V and a secondary voltage of 11.5 V. The secondary current is 4 A. Assuming 100% efficiency, calculate the primary current.
A transformer steps down from 240 V to 12 V. The secondary current is 4 A and the primary current is 0.25 A. Calculate the efficiency of the transformer.

bronze.display: A transformer has 1000 primary turns and 50 secondary turns. The primary voltage is 230 V. Calculate the secondary voltage.
A transformer has a primary voltage of 230 V and a secondary voltage of 12 V. The primary coil has 460 turns. Calculate the number of secondary turns.
A transformer has 500 primary turns and 2000 secondary turns. The primary voltage is 25 V. Calculate the secondary voltage.

misconceptions.message: Vs = 25 × (2000/500) = 25 × 4 = 100 V. More secondary turns = higher voltage (step-up).

bronze.display: A transformer has 1200 primary turns and 60 secondary turns. The primary voltage is 240 V. Calculate the secondary voltage.

misconceptions.message: Vs = 240 × (60/1200) = 240 × 0.05 = 12 V. Fewer secondary turns = lower voltage (step-down).

bronze.display: A transformer has 400 primary turns. The primary voltage is 230 V and the secondary voltage is 11.5 V. How many secondary turns does it have?
A transformer has 200 primary turns and 800 secondary turns. Is this a step-up or step-down transformer? Enter 'step-up' or 'step-down'.

misconceptions.message: More secondary turns (800) than primary (200) means the voltage is stepped UP. This is a step-up transformer.

bronze.display: A transformer has 600 primary turns and 300 secondary turns. The primary voltage is 120 V. Calculate the secondary voltage.
A transformer has 4000 primary turns and 200 secondary turns. Is this a step-up or step-down transformer? Enter 'step-up' or 'step-down'.

misconceptions.message: Fewer secondary turns (200) than primary (4000) means the voltage is stepped DOWN. This is a step-down transformer.

silver.display: A transformer has a primary voltage of 230 V and a secondary voltage of 11.5 V. The secondary current is 4 A. Calculate the primary current (assuming 100% efficiency).

misconceptions.message: Step-down transformer: lower voltage on secondary means HIGHER current. Ip < Is.

silver.display: A step-up transformer has 500 primary turns and 10,000 secondary turns. The primary voltage is 25 V and the primary current is 20 A. Calculate the secondary current (assuming 100% efficiency).

misconceptions.message: Step-up increases voltage but decreases current. Is = 1 A, not 400 A.

silver.display: A transformer has a primary voltage of 230 V, primary current 0.5 A, and secondary voltage of 23 V. Calculate the secondary current (assuming 100% efficiency).
A transformer steps down from 11,000 V to 220 V. The primary coil has 5000 turns. Calculate the number of secondary turns.
A transformer steps down from 11,000 V to 220 V. The secondary current is 40 A. Calculate the primary current (assuming 100% efficiency).

misconceptions.message: Step-down: lower V means higher I on secondary. Primary current is much smaller.

silver.display: A charger has a secondary voltage of 6 V and secondary current of 2 A. The primary current is 0.1 A. Calculate the primary voltage (assuming 100% efficiency).

gold.display: A power station generates 25 MW at 25,000 V. A step-up transformer increases the voltage to 400,000 V. The cables have a total resistance of 10 Ω. Calculate the power lost in the cables at 400,000 V. Give your answer to 1 decimal place in kW.

misconceptions.message: First find current: I = P/V = 25,000,000/400,000 = 62.5 A. Then loss = I²R = 62.5² × 10 = 39,062.5 W = 39.1 kW.
Power loss = I²R. Don't forget to square the current: 62.5² = 3906.25.

gold.display: A power station generates 25 MW at 25,000 V. The cables have a resistance of 10 Ω. Calculate the power lost in the cables if the electricity is transmitted at 25,000 V (without a step-up transformer). Give your answer in MW.

misconceptions.message: At 25 kV: I = P/V = 25,000,000/25,000 = 1000 A. Loss = I²R = 1000² × 10 = 10,000,000 W = 10 MW. That's 40% of total power wasted!
Power loss = I²R. Current is SQUARED — this is why high currents waste so much energy.

gold.display: A transformer steps down 240 V to 12 V. The secondary current is 4 A and the primary current is 0.25 A. Calculate the efficiency of the transformer as a percentage.

misconceptions.message: Power out = 12 × 4 = 48 W. Power in = 240 × 0.25 = 60 W. Efficiency = (48/60) × 100 = 80%.
Efficiency = output ÷ input × 100. Output power (48 W) is always less than input (60 W).

gold.display: A transformer needs to produce 9 V from a 230 V mains supply. If the secondary coil has 36 turns, how many primary turns are needed?

misconceptions.message: Step-down: primary needs MORE turns. np/ns = Vp/Vs = 230/9.

gold.display: A power station generates electricity at 25,000 V. A step-up transformer with 500 primary turns increases this to 400,000 V. Calculate the number of secondary turns.

misconceptions.message: Step-up: more secondary turns. The ratio is 400,000/25,000 = 16.

gold.display: A transformer is 90% efficient. The primary voltage is 230 V and the primary current is 2 A. The secondary voltage is 20 V. Calculate the secondary current. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

misconceptions.message: Input power = 230 × 2 = 460 W. Output power = 460 × 0.9 = 414 W. Is = 414 ÷ 20 = 20.7 A.
Don't assume 100% efficiency. Output power = input power × efficiency = 460 × 0.9 = 414 W.
